characters: A group of children sweeping, counting, drawing, singing, reading, playing and resting with their families through a week.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively, rhythmic voice; the days are said clearly and slowly
narrationPlan.pace: Lively, like a marching song (about 75 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A marching drum beat with a simple tune that goes up through the week and rests on Sunday (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian children also know the Akan day-names (such as Kwasi for a boy and Akosua for a girl born on Sunday) given by birth day. This song does not use them, but teachers may add the home-language names for the days.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the song fits a Ghanaian school week and does not favour any religion on Sunday or Friday.
Confirm the order of the days from Monday to Sunday.

pages.brief: Warm hand-painted gouache scene, landscape 4:3, following the character notes exactly. Children sweep a classroom and count pebbles. Keep a calm, uncluttered area for text.
pages.narration: March on the spot to the beat.

pages.brief: Warm hand-painted gouache scene, landscape 4:3, following the character notes exactly. Children draw pictures and sing in a circle. Keep a calm, uncluttered area for text.
pages.narration: Move your hand like a crayon, then sing.

pages.brief: Warm hand-painted gouache scene, landscape 4:3, following the character notes exactly. Two children read a book and then play outdoors. Keep a calm, uncluttered area for text.
pages.narration: Open your hands like a book, then run on the spot.

pages.brief: Warm hand-painted gouache scene, landscape 4:3, following the character notes exactly. A family sitting together under a tree. Keep a calm, uncluttered area for text.
pages.narration: Slow down, then clap to start the week again.

pages.brief: Warm hand-painted gouache scene, landscape 4:3, following the character notes exactly. Seven small circles in a row, one for each day. Keep a calm, uncluttered area for text.
pages.narration: Count on your fingers, then shout Whee!

teacherGuide.overview: A song for learning the seven days in order. Form: four couplets and a counting chorus. Rhyming pairs: floor/more, two/you, friend/end, near/here, me/Whee. It practises sequencing and rhyme.
learningGoals: Say the days of the week in order.
Link each day to a real activity.

subjectLinks.subject: English Language
subjectLinks.link: Rhyme and days of the week

beforeReading: Ask: what day is it today? What day was yesterday?
whileReading: March in place. Stop and point to the day on a wall chart at each page.
afterReading: Make a seven-box chart and draw what you did each day.
Sing the song again, changing the activities.
discussion: What do you do on school days?
What do you like to do on Saturday?
reflection: Which day of the week do you help at home?

mathsExtension.task: If today is Wednesday, what day is it in two days?
How many days are in two weeks?

support: Use a picture calendar and point to each day as it is sung.
stretch: Write a new couplet for a day of your choice.

culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian children also know the Akan day-names (such as Kwasi for a boy and Akosua for a girl born on Sunday) given by birth day. This song does not use them, but teachers may add the home-language names for the days.
localiseThis: Let children bring the names of the days in their home languages.
